sub_modules.title: Mendelian Genetics: Segregation, Independent Assortment & Probability Laws
sub_modules.overview: Gregor Mendel's particulate theory of inheritance (1865) established that discrete hereditary units (alleles at genetic loci) segregate equally into gametes during meiosis I and assort independently when located on non-homologous chromosomes.

core_concepts.heading: Mendel's Laws & Cytological Meiotic Correlates
core_concepts.theory: According to the Chromosome Theory of Inheritance (Sutton and Boveri, 1902), Mendel's abstract laws map directly onto the physical behavior of homologous chromosomes during Meiosis I. In a monohybrid cross (Aa × Aa), gametes receive either A or a with equal probability (p = 0.5), producing a 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa genotypic ratio and a 3:1 dominant-to-recessive phenotypic ratio.
key_principles: First Law (Law of Equal Segregation): Two alleles at a single diploid locus separate during Anaphase I of meiosis so that each haploid gamete carries exactly one allele.

Second Law (Law of Independent Assortment): Unlinked loci (or distant loci ≥50 cM apart on the same chromosome) align randomly at the Metaphase I equatorial plate, yielding four equiprobable gametes (1/4 AB : 1/4 Ab : 1/4 aB : 1/4 ab) and a 9:3:3:1 dihybrid F2 phenotypic ratio.

Testcross Verification: Crossing an individual of dominant phenotype (A_B_) to a homozygous recessive tester (aabb) directly reveals the gametic frequencies of the dominant parent (1:1:1:1 if unlinked; skewed toward parental classes if linked).

core_concepts.heading: Combinatorial Probability & Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit
core_concepts.theory: Predicting multi-locus genetic outcomes relies on the Product Rule (independent events occurring together: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)), the Sum Rule (mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)), and Binomial Expansion for unordered progeny families.
key_principles: Scaling with Heterozygous Loci (n): An individual heterozygous at n unlinked loci produces 2^n distinct gamete genotypes, 3^n distinct F2 zygotic genotypes, and 2^n distinct phenotypes (assuming complete dominance).

Chi-Square (χ²) Statistical Validation: Tests whether deviations between observed progeny counts (O) and Mendelian expected counts (E) are attributable to random sampling chance (Null Hypothesis H0 accepted if p > 0.05) or a biological distortion such as linkage, lethality, or epistasis (H0 rejected if p < 0.05), with degrees of freedom df = k - 1 (where k = number of phenotypic classes).

sub_modules.title: Advanced Genetics: Allelic Dominance, Epistasis, Linkage & Recombination Mapping
sub_modules.overview: Classical Mendelian ratios are modified by single-locus allelic interactions (incomplete dominance, codominance, lethality), multi-locus biochemical pathway interactions (epistasis), and physical chromosomal linkage.

core_concepts.heading: Dominance Series, Epistasis & Complementation Analysis
core_concepts.theory: Dominance is not an intrinsic property of an allele alone, but a reflection of how haplosufficient or haploinsufficient its protein product is within a biochemical or structural pathway. Epistasis occurs when alleles at one locus mask or modify the phenotypic expression of alleles at a second locus.
key_principles: Incomplete Dominance vs. Codominance: In incomplete dominance (e.g., Antirrhinum flower color), the heterozygote (CRCW) exhibits an intermediate dosage phenotype (pink), shifting the F2 phenotypic ratio to 1:2:1. In codominance (e.g., human ABO IAIB blood group or MN antigens), both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed on the cell surface.

Complementation Test (cis-trans Test - Seymour Benzer): Crosses two independent recessive mutants with the same mutant phenotype (m1/m1 × m2/m2). If the F1 trans-heterozygote is wild-type, the mutations complement and reside in different genes (cistrons); if the F1 remains mutant, the mutations fail to complement and are allelic (same gene).

core_concepts.heading: Chromosomal Linkage, Three-Point Testcrosses & Interference
core_concepts.theory: Genes located close together on the same chromosome violate Mendel's Second Law and co-segregate unless separated by a chiasma (homologous crossover) between non-sister chromatids during Pachytene of Prophase I. Alfred Sturtevant (1913) demonstrated that Recombination Frequency (RF) is proportional to physical distance along a linear chromosome.
key_principles: Coupling (cis) vs. Repulsion (trans) Phase: In coupling (AB / ab), parental gametes are AB and ab; in repulsion (Ab / aB), parental gametes are Ab and aB. Regardless of phase, Recombinant gametes always occur at ≤50% total frequency.

Maximum 50% Recombination Ceiling: Even if a crossover occurs in 100% of tetrads between two loci, each single crossover involves only 2 of the 4 chromatids, yielding 50% parental and 50% recombinant gametes (indistinguishable from independent assortment).

Three-Point Mapping & Chiasma Interference: In a trihybrid testcross (ABC / abc × abc / abc), the 8 progeny classes group into 4 pairs: the most frequent pair is Parental (NCO), the least frequent pair is Double Crossover (DCO), and comparing NCO vs. DCO reveals the middle gene. Positive chiasma interference (I = 1 - CoC > 0) occurs when one crossover physically inhibits a second crossover nearby.

sub_modules.title: Human Genetics: Pedigree Analysis, Non-Mendelian Inheritance & Genetic Counseling
sub_modules.overview: Because controlled experimental crosses are impossible in humans, medical genetics relies on multi-generation pedigree reconstruction, Bayesian conditional probability, and cytogenetic/molecular diagnostics.

core_concepts.heading: Mendelian Pedigree Modes & Diagnostic Hallmarks
core_concepts.theory: Human genetic traits follow five primary transmission patterns depending on whether the locus resides on an autosome (Chromosomes 1–22), the X or Y sex chromosomes, or the maternal mitochondrial genome (mtDNA).
key_principles: Autosomal Recessive (AR - e.g., Cystic Fibrosis, Sickle-Cell, PKU): Typically skips generations; unaffected heterozygous carrier parents (Aa × Aa) have a 1/4 risk of an affected child; incidence increases with consanguinity (first-cousin marriage coefficient of inbreeding F = 1/16).

Autosomal Dominant (AD - e.g., Huntington's Disease, Achondroplasia, Marfan Syndrome): Appears in every generation (vertical transmission); every affected child has at least one affected parent (unless a de novo mutation occurred); equal male-to-female transmission including father-to-son.

X-Linked Recessive (XR - e.g., Hemophilia A/B, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Red-Green Colorblindness): Affects hemizygous males (X^aY) predominantly; never transmitted from father to son (fathers pass Y to sons); affected males transmit the allele to 100% of their daughters (obligate carriers), who pass it to 50% of their sons.

X-Linked Dominant (XD - e.g., Rett Syndrome, Hypophosphatemic Rickets) vs. Mitochondrial (Maternal): In XD, affected fathers pass the trait to 100% of daughters and 0% of sons. In Mitochondrial inheritance (e.g., LHON, MERRF), affected mothers transmit the trait to 100% of offspring (with variable heteroplasmy), whereas affected fathers transmit to 0% of offspring.

core_concepts.heading: Incomplete Penetrance, Variable Expressivity & Bayesian Counseling
core_concepts.theory: Not all individuals with a disease-predisposing genotype manifest the clinical phenotype identically.
key_principles: Penetrance vs. Expressivity: Penetrance (P) is an all-or-none population probability—the percentage of individuals with a specific genotype who exhibit the phenotype at all (e.g., 80% penetrance means 20% of Aa individuals are phenotypically normal). Expressivity describes the severity or anatomical spectrum among affected individuals (e.g., Neurofibromatosis Type 1).

Bayesian Risk Revision in Genetic Counseling: Incorporates conditional phenotypic evidence (such as a prospective carrier mother already having 3 unaffected sons, or passing a certain age without symptoms) to update Prior Probability into Posterior Probability: P(Carrier | Data) = Joint_Carrier / (Joint_Carrier + Joint_NonCarrier).

sub_modules.title: Population Genetics: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium, Drift & Natural Selection
sub_modules.overview: Population genetics models microevolution as changes in allele frequencies (p, q) and genotype frequencies (p², 2pq, q²) within a Mendelian gene pool driven by non-random mating, mutation, migration, genetic drift, and natural selection.

core_concepts.heading: The Hardy-Weinberg Principle & Inbreeding Deviations
core_concepts.theory: Formulated independently by G.H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg (1908), in an infinitely large, randomly mating (panmictic) diploid population free from mutation, migration (gene flow), and natural selection, allele frequencies (p + q = 1) remain constant across generations, and genotype frequencies reach stable equilibrium (p² AA : 2pq Aa : q² aa) after a single generation of random mating.
key_principles: Five Assumptions of HWE: (1) Infinite population size (no genetic drift); (2) Random mating (no assortative mating or inbreeding); (3) No net mutation; (4) No migration/gene flow; (5) No natural selection (equal viability and fertility across all genotypes).

Wright's Inbreeding Coefficient (F): Inbreeding (consanguinity or self-pollination) does not alter allele frequencies (p and q remain unchanged), but systematically reduces heterozygosity (H = 2pq(1 - F)) while increasing homozygosity (P_AA = p² + pqF; P_aa = q² + pqF). Complete selfing (as in Mendel's peas or Arabidopsis) halves heterozygosity every generation.

core_concepts.heading: Evolutionary Forces: Natural Selection, Balancing Selection & Genetic Drift
core_concepts.theory: When HWE assumptions are violated, allele frequencies change predictably (directional/balancing selection, migration) or stochastically (genetic drift).
key_principles: Relative Fitness (w) & Selection Coefficient (s = 1 - w): Selection against a recessive lethal allele (w_aa = 0, s = 1) reduces q slowly at low frequencies because most recessive alleles are hidden from selection inside phenotypically normal heterozygotes (2pq >> q²).

Heterozygote Advantage (Overdominance / Balancing Selection): When the heterozygote has higher fitness than either homozygote (w_AA = 1 - s1, w_Aa = 1, w_aa = 1 - s2, e.g., HbA/HbS sickle-cell trait in Plasmodium falciparum malaria regions), allele frequencies converge to a stable polymorphic equilibrium: q̂ = s1 / (s1 + s2).

Genetic Drift & Effective Population Size (Ne): Random sampling error in finite populations causes neutral alleles to fix (probability of fixation = initial frequency p0) or go extinct, eroding heterozygosity at a rate of 1 / (2Ne) per generation.

sub_modules.title: Plant Genetics: Marker-Assisted Selection, QTL Mapping & Quantitative Inheritance
sub_modules.overview: As a flagship Cellulum module, Plant Genetics integrates polygenic quantitative trait architecture (heritability, additive vs. dominance variance) with molecular marker technologies (SSR, SNP, QTL mapping) to accelerate crop improvement.

core_concepts.heading: Quantitative Trait Architecture, Heritability & Response to Selection
core_concepts.theory: Agronomic traits such as grain yield, drought tolerance, plant height, and oil content are continuous (polygenic/quantitative) traits controlled by multiple Quantitative Trait Loci (QTLs) plus environmental effects: Phenotypic Variance (V_P) partitions into Genetic Variance (V_G = V_A + V_D + V_I) and Environmental Variance (V_E).
key_principles: Broad-Sense (H²) vs. Narrow-Sense Heritability (h²): Broad-sense heritability (H² = V_G / V_P) measures total genetic contribution to phenotypic variance. Narrow-sense heritability (h² = V_A / V_P) isolates Additive Genetic Variance (V_A)—the only component reliably transmitted from parents to sexually reproduced progeny.

The Breeder's Equation (R = h² · S): Predicts the genetic gain or Response to Selection (R = mean of offspring - mean of parental population) from the Selection Differential (S = mean of selected parents - mean of parental population) and narrow-sense heritability (h²).

core_concepts.heading: Molecular Markers, QTL Mapping & Marker-Assisted Backcrossing (MABC)
core_concepts.theory: DNA markers provide environmentally invariant tags across the plant genome. By genotyping segregating populations—such as F2, Backcross (BC1), Doubled Haploids (DH), or Recombinant Inbred Lines (RILs)—breeders map QTLs using Logarithm of the Odds (LOD) scores and introgress elite alleles via Marker-Assisted Selection (MAS).
key_principles: Dominant vs. Co-Dominant Molecular Markers: RAPD and AFLP are dominant markers (cannot distinguish homozygote AA from heterozygote Aa without progeny testing). RFLP, SSR (Microsatellites), and SNPs (KASP/TaqMan/Genotyping-by-Sequencing) are co-dominant markers that resolve all three genotypes (AA, Aa, aa) in F2/BC populations.

QTL LOD Score Thresholds: The LOD score compares the likelihood that a trait locus and molecular marker are linked (at recombination fraction θ) versus unlinked (θ = 0.5): LOD = log10[L(θ) / L(0.5)]. A LOD score ≥ 3.0 indicates 1000:1 odds in favor of linkage.

Marker-Assisted Backcrossing (Foreground vs. Background Selection): Foreground selection uses flanking markers (<1–2 cM from target gene) to track the donor resistance/trait allele; Background selection uses genome-wide SNPs to accelerate recovery of the Recurrent Parent Genome (RPG), achieving >99% recurrent genome recovery in BC2–BC3 instead of BC6.

interactive_pins.detail: For any bi-allelic locus under random mating, heterozygote frequency never exceeds 50%, reaching its peak at p = q = 0.5 (where p² = 0.25, 2pq = 0.50, q² = 0.25).

interactive_pins.label: Rare Recessive Carrier Reservoir
interactive_pins.detail: When q = 0.01 (1 in 10,000 affected), 2pq ≈ 0.0198 (~1 in 50 carriers). Thus, 99% of all recessive alleles in the population reside silently inside heterozygous carriers.

Self-fertilization of the F1 plants yields 320 F2 progeny consisting of 189 purple-flowered plants and 131 white-flowered plants. (b) Perform a Chi-square (χ²) goodness-of-fit test against your proposed ratio and state whether the Null Hypothesis is accepted at α = 0.05 (given critical values: χ²_0.05,1 = 3.841; χ²_0.05,2 = 5.991; χ²_0.05,3 = 7.815).

practice_problems.question: In a cross between two tetrahybrid pea plants (AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd, where all 4 loci assort independently and exhibit complete dominance), what fraction of the F2 progeny is expected to have the genotype AabbCcDD, and what fraction will display the dominant phenotype for all 4 traits (A_B_C_D_)?
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: Using the Product Rule across independent monohybrid crosses: P(Aa) = 1/2, P(bb) = 1/4, P(Cc) = 1/2, P(DD) = 1/4. Multiplying gives (1/2)(1/4)(1/2)(1/4) = 1/64. For the dominant phenotype at all 4 loci, each locus has P(dominant) = 3/4, so (3/4)^4 = 81/256.

practice_problems.question: Two loci (M and N) are separated by a genetic map distance of 16.0 cM on the same chromosome. If a plant heterozygous in repulsion phase (M n / m N) is self-pollinated (assuming equal male and female recombination rates and no interference), what percentage of the F2 progeny will be homozygous recessive for both traits (mm nn)?
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: In repulsion phase (M n / m N), the gametes M n and m N are Parental (total 84%, or 42% each), while M N and m n are Recombinant (total 16.0%, so m n = 8.0% = 0.08). To produce an mm nn zygote upon selfing, a recombinant m n pollen grain (0.08) must fertilize a recombinant m n ovule (0.08): P(mm nn) = (0.08) × (0.08) = 0.0064 = 0.64%.

practice_problems.question: An autosomal dominant disorder has a penetrance of 60% (P = 0.60). If a heterozygous affected father (Aa) and a homozygous normal mother (aa) have a child, what is the probability that the child will clinically express the disorder?
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: The Mendelian probability that the child inherits the dominant allele (Aa) from the heterozygous father is 1/2 (0.50). Multiplying the probability of inheriting the genotype (0.50) by the probability of penetrance (0.60) gives P(affected) = 0.50 × 0.60 = 0.30 (30%).

case_study.title: Translational Genetics Case Study: The Bombay Phenotype (hh Epistasis) & Sub1A Marker-Assisted Rice Breeding
case_study.scenario: Case A (Human Epistasis): A woman with blood type O and a man with blood type A have a daughter with blood type AB, prompting a paternity dispute—yet DNA microsatellite profiling confirms 99.999% paternity. Investigation reveals the mother is homozygous for the rare FUT1 (hh) mutation ('Bombay Phenotype'). Case B (Plant MAS): Breeders at IRRI introgressed the Sub1A ethylene-response-factor QTL from the low-yielding Indian landrace FR13A into the high-yielding mega-variety Swarna using SSR foreground, recombinant, and background markers.
case_study.mechanistic_analysis: In Case A, the FUT1 (H) locus encodes α-1,2-fucosyltransferase, which synthesizes the H-antigen oligosaccharide precursor required for the ABO glycosyltransferases (IA and IB) to attach N-acetylgalactosamine or galactose. Because the mother is genotypically hh IB IB (or IB i), she cannot synthesize H-antigen and types phenotypically as group O on standard hemagglutination assays, even though she transmits an active IB allele to her daughter (who inherits a functional H allele from her IA father, producing Hh IA IB = type AB). This is a classic human example of Recessive Epistasis (9:3:4). In Case B, tightly linked flanking SSR markers eliminated 'linkage drag' around the Sub1A locus on Chromosome 9 while genome-wide background SSRs recovered >98% of the Swarna genome in just 2–3 backcrosses, creating 'Swarna-Sub1'—which survives 14 days of complete flash-flood submergence without yield penalty.

quiz.question: Why can the observed Recombination Frequency (RF) between two loci on the same chromosome never exceed 50%, even if their genetic map distance is 120 cM?
options: Chiasma interference prevents more than one crossover from occurring on any chromosome

Each single crossover event in a meiotic tetrad involves only 2 of the 4 sister chromatids, and multiple crossovers randomize outer markers equally between parental and recombinant configurations (yielding a 1:1 limit = 50%)
DNA Polymerase δ repairs all crossovers that exceed 50 cM during Pachytene
Loci separated by more than 50 cM translocate to non-homologous chromosomes
quiz.explanation: In any meiotic tetrad where at least one crossover occurs between two loci, averaging across single, double, triple, and quadruple crossovers involving 2, 3, or 4 chromatids mathematically converges to a 1:1 ratio of parental-to-recombinant chromatids (50% maximum RF), whereas map distance (cM) sums additive short intervals.

quiz.question: If a plant population undergoes continuous self-pollination (F -> 1) over several generations in the absence of selection, mutation, or migration, how do allele frequencies (p and q) and genotype frequencies (AA, Aa, aa) change?
options: Both allele frequencies and heterozygote frequency decrease by 50% each generation
Allele frequencies (p and q) remain strictly constant, while heterozygote frequency (2pq) decreases by 50% each generation and splits equally into AA and aa homozygotes
The recessive allele q is eliminated from the population, leaving 100% AA homozygotes
Heterozygote frequency increases to 100% due to hybrid vigor
quiz.explanation: Self-fertilization (inbreeding) only rearranges alleles into genotypes without removing or adding alleles to the gene pool. In each selfing generation, AA × AA -> 100% AA and aa × aa -> 100% aa, while Aa × Aa produces 1/4 AA + 1/2 Aa + 1/4 aa, halving heterozygosity every generation while keeping p and q constant.

quiz.question: In a human pedigree, an affected mother transmits a rare genetic disorder to 100% of her sons and 100% of her daughters, whereas an affected father transmits the disorder to 0% of his sons and 0% of his daughters. What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
quiz.explanation: Because the oocyte contributes virtually 100% of the zygote's cytoplasm and mitochondria (while paternal sperm mitochondria are eliminated via ubiquitin-mediated mitophagy after fertilization), mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are transmitted exclusively from affected mothers to all offspring, and never from affected fathers.

research_corner.paper_title: The Linear Arrangement of Six Sex-Linked Factors in Drosophila, as Shown by Their Mode of Association (Sturtevant, 1913) & Sub1A is an Ethylene-Response-Factor-Like Gene that Confers Submergence Tolerance to Rice (Xu et al., Nature 2006)

imrad_breakdown.abstract_summary: Sturtevant (1913), working as an undergraduate in T.H. Morgan's Fly Room, used recombination frequencies from three-point crosses to construct the world's first genetic linkage map. Xu et al. (2006) fine-mapped the Sub1 locus in rice using 4,022 F2 segregants and positional cloning to identify Sub1A-1, enabling precision Marker-Assisted Backcrossing into mega-varieties.
imrad_breakdown.key_method: Three-point testcross recombination scoring in Drosophila melanogaster; high-resolution SSR/CAPS/SNP recombinant breakpoint mapping and transgenic complementation in Oryza sativa.
imrad_breakdown.critical_takeaway: Recombination frequency is an additive metric over short chromosomal intervals (1 cM = 1% recombination), providing the mathematical foundation for positional cloning, QTL mapping, and modern genomic breeding.
